name: Chia seeds
summary: Chia seeds are tiny seeds of a plant from Mexico and Central America, eaten whole, soaked in liquid or ground. This page lists what people say chia seeds do; each claim can be checked against the research when you choose.
inIt: Chia seeds are a rich source of alpha-linolenic acid, a plant omega-3 fat: about 65 % of the seed oil, according to a 2016 review.
They hold a lot of dietary fibre, plus protein without gluten, vitamins, minerals and plant compounds such as chlorogenic acid, caffeic acid, quercetin and kaempferol.

The UK food table (CoFID) has no entry for chia seeds, so this page gives no per-100 g figures from it. Plant compounds like the ones above are not measured in food tables, which cover about 150 nutrients.
processing: Chia seeds are eaten whole, soaked or ground. The 2019 review covers how the seeds are used in food production; this page does not claim that grinding or soaking changes what the body takes up.

whoShouldBeCareful.with: Allergy to sesame or other seeds
whoShouldBeCareful.note: A 2026 review says chia seed is a potential emerging food allergen, with case reports of immediate allergic reactions and anaphylaxis, and that its proteins can be recognised by the antibodies of people allergic to sesame. It also says this does not prove a person with sesame allergy will react to chia, and that it cannot give how common chia allergy is. If you have a seed allergy, talk to your doctor or an allergist.

unknowns: Whether eating chia seeds changes health outcomes in people: this page does not review the trials, and the reviews mix lab, animal and human findings.
How common chia seed allergy is, and who reacts: the 2026 review says the evidence cannot say.
How the plant omega-3 in chia seeds compares with the fish omega-3s (EPA and DHA) in the body: the food table does not measure it.
